system:
You are the reading pass of an illustration engine. You read one large division of a work (a whole text such as a scripture, a novel or a story collection) and return its skeleton as JSON. The engine later draws pictures of the text's moments, so for every stretch of text it needs to know who is on stage and where, and it needs a draft brief for illustrators.

The text comes as numbered units. Each unit line starts with its id (for example `17:4` or `[12]`). Lines starting with `##` are headings, not units.

Return:

1. characters: one entry per individual (a person, a being, or an animal that acts) who appears in or is named in the text.
   - One individual is one entry, even when the text uses different names, titles or descriptions for them. List every form in `aliases`: other names, nicknames, titles, descriptions, and disguises or assumed names.
   - Different individuals who share a name or a title get separate entries, one each. Never fold two people into one entry because they share a name. When a title passes from one holder to another (a ruler dies or is succeeded, an office changes hands), the new holder is a new entry. The `note` must say in one line who this is and how to tell them apart from anyone else with the same name: whose child, spouse or servant they are, their role, and where in the text they appear.
   - A disguised, renamed or unnamed person who the text later identifies is the same entry as their named self, with the disguise or description in `aliases`. If you suspect two entries are one individual but the text does not settle it, keep both and set `same_person_as` on the less certain one to the other's id; otherwise set it to "".
   - Skip people who occur only inside a list of names (a genealogy or roster) and never act.
   - Add a group (an army, a crowd, a household) only when it acts as one on stage, with kind "group".
2. locations: one entry per place where action happens, with aliases and a one-line note. Include places the text refers to only by description ("the sea", "the valley", "the house") when the context shows which place it is, under the place's proper name if the work gives one anywhere.
3. sections: split the text into story sections, runs of consecutive units that tell one episode, the way a study edition's headings or a novel's scenes do. Start a new section when the time, the place or the main action changes. Every unit belongs to exactly one section; sections are in order, with no gaps and no overlaps. This division has 1213 units. Aim for roughly 67 sections (54 to 80), averaging about 18 units each; some sections will be much shorter and some longer. Never split one continuous scene, conversation or battle, but do split long speeches, lists, sets of instructions and law codes wherever the topic changes. Give the ids of each section's first and last unit and a short title. For each section:
   - setting: ids of the locations where its action happens.
   - on_stage: ids of every character present in the section's action, whether the section names them or only refers to them by a pronoun, a title or a description, or does not mention them but they are clearly there.
   - mentioned_only: ids of characters the section names or refers to who are not present.
4. brief: a draft brief for illustrators, for this division only. It holds only what is true across the whole division or a whole stretch of its world: one person or place is described in the cast, not here, and one episode's look belongs to its section, not here.
   - tone: one line on the mood the pictures should carry.
   - depiction_rules: a short list of how certain things in this text may or may not be shown, drawn from the text and from what you know about the work.
   - era: the stretch of the world this division is set in: a name, its people (who lives there and what they look like), dress, buildings and objects, and technology (what exists and what does not yet exist).
   Keep the brief under 200 words.

Use short, stable snake_case ids (for example `david`, `the_queen`, `main_street`). Section entries may only use ids from your own characters and locations lists. Do not quote the text.

characters.name: Moses
aliases: the Hebrew baby drawn from the water
characters.note: Son of a Levite woman, raised in Pharaoh's household, flees to Midian, then leads Israel out of Egypt and receives the law on Sinai; appears from chapter 2 to the end.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.note: Moses' older brother and spokesman, later Israel's first high priest; appears from chapter 4 onward.

characters.name: Miriam
characters.note: Sister of Moses and Aaron who leads the women's song at the sea (15:20-21).

characters.name: Joshua
characters.note: Moses' young servant who fights Amalek and waits at the Tent; distinct from no one else in this division.

characters.name: Pharaoh
aliases: the new king who did not know Joseph
characters.note: The king of Egypt who enslaves Israel and orders the infant boys drowned; reigns in chapters 1-2 and dies by 2:23. Not to be confused with the later Pharaoh of the plagues.

characters.name: Pharaoh
characters.note: The successor king who confronts Moses and Aaron, suffers the plagues, and pursues Israel to the Red Sea; appears from chapter 5 to chapter 15.

characters.name: Pharaoh's daughter
characters.note: Daughter of the first Pharaoh who finds Moses in the reeds and adopts him; appears only in chapter 2.

characters.name: Shiphrah
characters.note: One of the two Hebrew midwives who defy the king's order; appears only in chapter 1.

characters.name: Puah
characters.note: The other Hebrew midwife who defies the king's order; appears only in chapter 1.

characters.name: Moses' mother
aliases: the woman of the house of Levi
characters.note: Unnamed Levite woman who hides her baby, sets him in the basket, and nurses him back; appears in chapter 2.

characters.name: Moses' sister
characters.note: Unnamed sister who watches the basket and fetches their mother as nurse; appears in chapter 2.

characters.name: Jethro
characters.note: Priest of Midian, father of Zipporah, who hosts Moses and later counsels him on judging the people (chapters 2-4 and 18).

characters.name: Zipporah
characters.note: Midianite wife of Moses who circumcises their son at a lodging place (chapters 2, 4, 18).

characters.name: Gershom
characters.note: Moses and Zipporah's son, named for Moses' exile; appears in chapters 2 and 18 and is only named otherwise.

characters.name: Eliezer
characters.note: Moses' second son, named in chapter 18 for God's help against Pharaoh; mentioned only.

characters.name: Amalek
characters.note: The people who fight Israel at Rephidim; appear as a hostile group in chapter 17.

characters.name: the children of Israel
characters.note: The whole Hebrew people, who act together as a crowd throughout the division.

characters.name: the Egyptians
characters.note: Egyptian overseers, soldiers and magicians who act as a group in the oppression and pursuit.

characters.name: Yahweh
characters.note: The god of Israel who speaks to Moses from the bush, sends plagues, leads by pillar of cloud and fire, and gives the law; a divine presence shown as voice, fire, cloud or glory.

characters.name: Bezalel
characters.note: Chief craftsman of the tabernacle, of the tribe of Judah, filled with the spirit of God (chapters 31, 35-38).

characters.name: Oholiab
characters.note: Craftsman of the tribe of Dan who works with Bezalel on the tabernacle (chapters 31, 35-38).

characters.name: the elders of Israel
characters.note: Israel's elders who are gathered, believe the signs, and go up the mountain with Moses and Aaron (chapters 3-4, 18, 24).

characters.name: Nadab and Abihu
characters.note: Aaron's older sons, who see God on the mountain and are later named as priests; mentioned in 6:23, 24:1, 24:9, 28:1, 29 and 40.

characters.name: Eleazar and Ithamar
characters.note: Aaron's younger sons, named as priests-in-training and for the tabernacle accounts (6:23, 28:1, 38:21).

characters.name: Hur
aliases: the man who holds up Moses' hands
characters.note: Helper who holds up Moses' hands in the battle with Amalek (17:10-12) and is left in charge with Aaron (24:14).

characters.name: Korah
characters.note: Levite named only in a genealogy (6:21, 6:24); no action.

characters.name: the sons of Levi
characters.note: The tribe of Levi, who gather to Moses and carry out the slaughter after the golden calf (32:26-28).

characters.name: the people at the calf
aliases: the people who made the calf
characters.note: The Israelites who gather to Aaron, give their gold and dance before the molten calf (32:1-6, 33:4-6).

locations.name: Egypt
locations.note: The land of slavery and the setting of the plagues and the Passover night.; actions occur at the cities of Pithom, Raamses and Goshen within it.

locations.name: Goshen
locations.note: The Egyptian region where the Israelites live apart from the plagues (8:22, 9:26).

locations.name: the river Nile
locations.note: The river where the infant Moses is set adrift and the first plague turns its water to blood.

locations.name: Midian
locations.note: The desert land where Moses flees, meets Jethro's daughters, and receives his call.

locations.name: Mount Sinai
locations.note: The mountain where God appears in the bush (3:1), gives the law and the tablets, and where the calf is made at its foot.

locations.name: the Red Sea
locations.note: The sea that Israel crosses on dry ground while the Egyptian army drowns.

locations.name: the wilderness
locations.note: The desert between Egypt and Sinai where Israel wanders, is fed with manna, and is tested.

locations.name: the camp of Israel
aliases: the Tent of Meeting outside the camp
locations.note: The encampment where the people gather, quarrel, murmur and where the Tent is set up.

locations.name: Rephidim
locations.note: The stopping place where water is drawn from the rock and Amalek attacks (17:1-16).

locations.name: the tabernacle
locations.note: The portable sanctuary described in chapters 25-31 and set up in chapter 40.

brief.tone: Awe and dread alternating with stark human struggle: the sublime power of God and the grit of slavery and wilderness.
depiction_rules: Show God only through fire, cloud, light, glory or the bush, never as a human form.
Depict the plagues vividly but without gratuitous gore; the Red Sea should show walls of water rather than a melee.
The golden calf and the Levite slaughter may be shown as aftermath or ritual dance but avoid lingering on violence.
Moses' shining face should be a visible glow or light, not a mask.
Keep the tabernacle plans precise and consistent with the described materials (acacia, gold, blue-purple-scarlet linen, cherubim).

era.name: Late Bronze Age Egypt and the Sinai wilderness, c. 1450-1200 BCE (traditional reckoning)
era.people: Egyptians with shaved heads or wigs, kilts and collars, and Semitic Hebrew shepherds and laborers in simple tunics and cloaks; Midianite herders in the desert.
era.dress: Linen kilts and tunics for Egyptians; plain wool or linen robes and sandals for Israelites; Aaron's priestly garments of blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen with an ephod, breastplate and gold bells; Bezalel and Oholiab as skilled craftsmen in plain work clothes.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities such as Pithom and Raamses, mud-brick and stone temples, chariots, papyrus baskets sealed with pitch, clay ovens and kneading troughs; the tent of meeting and gold-overlaid acacia furnishings in the wilderness.
era.technology: Bronze and gold working, weaving and embroidery, chariots and horses, but no iron tools in the common sense of the text, no writing on paper, and only stone tablets for the law.
